nameStory: Despite its name, the Iceland Gull doesn't actually breed in Iceland at all! This medium-sized seabird got its common name because Iceland is one of the places where it regularly spends the winter months. The scientific name 'glaucoides' means 'resembling glaucous,' referring to its similarity to the larger Glaucous Gull.
description: The Iceland Gull is a graceful, medium-sized seabird that visits New England waters during winter months. These pale, elegant gulls are smaller and more delicate-looking than the common Herring Gulls you see year-round. They have a clean, almost ethereal appearance with very pale gray backs and wings, bright white heads and bodies, and relatively small, neat bills. Adults typically measure about the size of a Ring-billed Gull but with longer, more slender proportions.

idTips.label: Pale wing tips
idTips.description: The wing tips are very pale gray or nearly white, never the bold black found on Herring Gulls - this ghostly appearance is visible both in flight and when folded

idTips.label: Delicate build
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller-headed and more slender than Herring Gulls, with a gentler, almost dove-like expression and proportionally longer wings

idTips.label: Bill characteristics
idTips.description: Small, neat yellow bill (in adults) that looks proportionally smaller and more delicate than the chunky bills of larger gulls

idTips.label: Overall coloration
idTips.description: Extremely pale throughout - the back and wings are such a light pearl-gray they almost appear white in bright sunlight

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: More buoyant and tern-like in flight than other large gulls, with quicker wingbeats and a lighter, more graceful appearance

habitat: Iceland Gulls visit New England's coastal waters, harbors, and beaches during winter months. Look for them along rocky shores, in busy fishing ports where they scavenge, and around offshore islands. They're often found mixed in with flocks of more common gulls at fish processing plants, dumps near the coast, and anywhere food scraps are available.

seasonality.spring: Still present in early spring but becoming less common as they begin migrating north to Arctic breeding grounds by April and May.
seasonality.summer: Absent from New England during summer months, as they breed far north in Arctic Canada and Greenland.
seasonality.fall: Begin arriving in late fall, with November being the start of peak viewing season as they return from northern breeding areas.
seasonality.winter: Peak viewing time in New England - most easily found from December through March in harbors and along the coast.

funFact: Iceland Gulls are such strong fliers that they regularly cross the massive Greenland ice sheet during migration - a journey of hundreds of miles over solid ice with no place to land or feed!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the much larger Glaucous Gull, which also has pale wing tips. Remember: Iceland Gulls are noticeably smaller and more delicate, about the size of a Herring Gull, while Glaucous Gulls are massive - as big as Great Black-backed Gulls. Think 'petite and pale' for Iceland Gulls.
contextualKnowledge: The name is genuinely misleading - these gulls are only winter visitors to Iceland and don't breed there at all. Their true breeding grounds are in the high Arctic regions of Canada and Greenland, making their appearance in New England waters a special winter treat for birders.
compareHints: Among New England's large gulls, Iceland Gulls are unique for their combination of medium size and extremely pale wing tips. Herring Gulls have bold black wing tips, Great Black-backed Gulls have dark backs and wings, and Ring-billed Gulls are smaller with more distinct markings. Only the much larger Glaucous Gull shares the pale wing tip feature, but it's obviously bigger and bulkier.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's large gulls, American Herring Gulls are the 'Goldilocks' species - not as massive as Great Black-backed Gulls, not as small as Ring-billed Gulls, but just right in the middle.
Ring-billed Gulls are smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, lacking the Herring Gull's robust build and pink legs.

Among New England gulls, Great Black-backed Gulls dwarf the common Herring Gull in size and have much darker backs, while Ring-billed Gulls are significantly smaller with lighter grey backs and distinctive black rings around their bills.
Among the large white-headed gulls, Lesser Black-backed Gulls are distinguished by their uniquely dark backs - darker than Herring Gulls but not as massive as Great Black-backed Gulls.
Among New England's large gulls, Glaucous Gulls stand out for their pale wingtips—Herring Gulls and Great Black-backed Gulls both have bold black wingtips, while Ring-billed Gulls are much smaller.
Common Gulls are smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, with yellow-green (not orange-red) bills and legs, plus a gentler facial expression.
Compared to the common Herring Gull, the Slaty-backed Gull has a noticeably darker slate-gray back and is generally larger and more robust.
Unlike Ring-billed Gulls which have a black ring on a yellow bill, Black-tailed Gulls have a red spot and often a black band near the bill tip.
Compared to the common Ring-billed Gull, Short-billed Gulls are smaller with cleaner wing tips and lack any dark markings on the bill.
Among the large white-headed gulls in its genus, the California Gull is most similar to the Ring-billed and Herring Gulls but sits between them in size.
Unlike the common white-bodied gulls of New England like Herring and Ring-billed Gulls, Heermann's Gull has the reverse color scheme with a dark body and white head.
